Now the final thing I want to show you regarding list comprehensions is that there's also such a thing as a Conditional List Comprehension. This takes our keywords a little bit further, whereas previously we stopped right here, "new_item for item in list," we can also tag on two more keywords 'if' and a 'test'. What this is going to allow us to do is to only add this new item, and only to perform this code if the test actually passes. Here's an example. The item I can call it anything I want, I'll just call it name in terms of the singular form of names. And then once I loop through each of the names inside my list of names, what is the new item going to be? Well, it's actually going to be unmodified, it's just going to be that same name, but in this case I'm only going to add that name to the list if it passes this test. And this test is going to look at the length of the name which I created here, so if I named this n, then I would be testing it against n and I would be adding n as well, but because I've called it name, so I'm going to use that name right here in the condition. So if the length of the name is less than 5, so it has 4 or less characters, then I'm going to add that name to my new_list. Now when I hit Enter you can see that I've got this new list of short_names and it only contains the names, Alex, Beth, and Dave. So this list comprehension is now a little bit more complex because the first thing it does is it goes through each of the names inside this list of names, it checks each of those names for its length, and if the length is 5, then it adds the name to this new list. Now here's a challenge for you. ### How to use Dictionary Comprehension

Now that you've seen how list comprehension works, it's time to learn about another type of comprehension, dictionary comprehensions. This is also super useful because it allows us to create a new dictionary from the values in a list or in a dictionary. For example, we could write out our keywords like this. We're going to create a new dictionary called new_dict, and it's going to be created using this curly bracket now instead of square brackets. And inside the comprehension, we get to set the new_key, the new_value, and we get to loop through items in a list. So any sort of iterable; a list, a range, a string, anything you want. And this is the simplest form of dictionary comprehension. Now remember that a dictionary comprehension is just a way of creating a dictionary using this shortened syntax. We could take this one step further. We could also create a new dictionary based on the values in an existing dictionary. So we could take that dictionary and then get hold of all of the items inside that dictionary, and then split it into a key and a value. So now, we're looping through each of the keys and each of the values in all of the items from the dictionary, and we can use these key and value variables to create a new_key or a new_value. And to go one step further for completion sake, we can, of course, as always add our condition at the very end, just like we did before with list comprehensions. So let's see how this code works in practice. ### How to Iterate over a Pandas DataFrame

In this lesson, I want to show you how you can use loops with pandas dataframes and how to iterate over a pandas data frame. So here, I've got a simple dictionary, I've got two keys, student and score, and under student I've got a list of student names, and under score I've got a list of their corresponding scores. Now we know that we can loop through a dictionary very simply by creating a for loop and then we say, well, we're going to go through each of the key and values inside this student dictionary. And then we're going to get all of the items in order to be able to loop through it. So now when I print each of the keys, you can see that it goes through the dictionary and prints both of the keys. And similarly, I can get it to loop through both of the values. So this is how we've been looping through dictionaries and we've been using it in our dictionary comprehension. Now you can loop through a data frame in the same way that you loop through a dictionary. In a lot of ways, you can consider a data frame pretty much as if you're working with a Python dictionary. So I'm going to go ahead and import pandas and I'm going to use pandas to create a new data frame, and it's going to be created from our student dictionary. So you've seen all of this before, and I'll just call this the student_data_frame and I can print it for you to see what it looks like. Okay. This is our data frame. It looks like a pretty standard table with the first column being all of the indices. So at zero index is this first row, and that basically denotes the index of each row. Now working with this data frame, we can actually loop through a data frame using the same method as before. So we can say for key, value in our student_data_frame .items. So if I print each of the keys, you can see it's just going to give me the titles of each column. But if I print each of the values, then it's going to give me the data in each of the columns. Now this is not particularly useful because it's basically just looping through the names of our columns and then the data inside each column. This is why pandas has a inbuilt loop and it's a method called iterrows. And it allows us to loop through each of the rows of the data frame rather than each of the columns. And the way that we do that is we again use a for loop and then we can get hold of each of the index inside each row, so that corresponds to the number in that first column. And then we can get hold of the data in the row. And then we can say for index row in data frame, which is student_data_frame, and then its that method.iter rows. And now I can loop through each of those rows and print out either the index for each of those rows. So you can see that this is going to print out our data frame here, And then in order to print out each of the index at 0, 1, 2. But I can also print out each of the rows. So now I get the first row has a student and a score, the second row has a student and a score, and the third row has a student and score. So each of these rows is a pandas series object. So that means we can tap into the row and then get hold of the value under a particular column by using the dot notation. So we can say row.student and now when it goes through the loop, you can see first, it's going to print out our entire data frame, and then it's going to print out each of the students inside that data frame. Now I can also say row.score, and now it's going to give me each of the scores inside the data frame. And I can even do something like this where I say if the row.student is equal to Angela, well then we can print that particular row that we're currently looping on, .score. And this way we would get the student, Angela's score which happens to be 56, as you can verify here.

### Introducing the NATO Alphabet Project

Now we're finally ready to tackle our project, and this project is based on a real-life struggle that I have. Often when I'm calling a company and over the phone I have to give some sort of details right? They'll ask me, what is your name, and can you spell it? So I'll have to be like A-N-G-E-L-A. And they're like, wait, was that an E? Was that a B, what did you say? In these cases often I have to sort of default to some sort of Naval alphabet. where I say A is the alfa, N for November, G for golf. And then at some point I forget what E stands for and I'm like E for.. elephant? And there have been times where I've just completely taken the MIG and said things like M for mnemonic, P for pneumonia, W for wrench, which doesn't make any sense at all because these are silent letters. And I've had some very angry people, um, but it was quite fun. So now what we want to create is we want to create a tool that takes the NATO phonetic alphabet which was generated because it's often really, really important for the other side to know exactly what it is that you said and which letters you're spelling out so that they don't mistaken your E for a B or your T for a C cause it all sounds really similar. Head over to the course resources page where you can find the starting files for the NATO alphabet project. I want you to practice with list comprehension and with dictionary comprehension. But in this case, we're not going through a dictionary per se, but we're actually going through a data frame because our data lives inside a CSV. So we're going to be reading it using pandas. and then we're going to end up with a data frame. Instead of having a bog standard dictionary comprehension where our keywords were new_key: new_value for key, value in dict.items. Now, GUIs were a huge deal back in the nineties because previously, in order to interact with a computer, you had to use a command line operating system such as MS-DOS. So this is kind of similar to our Python console, where everything we wanted the computer to do we had to tell it by writing a piece of text. So if we wanted Python to print hello, we have to write out the text. But GUIs were different. GUIs are graphical, and accompanied with a mouse, they allow a user with very little training in computers to be able to just point and click on the thing that they want to do on the screen. And one of the earliest computers that incorporated this type of GUI operating system was the Mac Lisa. It had these little windows which you can click on and it launches programs, which you can interact with by pointing and clicking. Now, I mentioned that the Mac had these windows and in fact, the Mac had programmed windows before Windows actually existed. So Windows was Microsoft's version of the graphical user interface operating system. And when it first came out, it created quite a bit of controversy because it seemed like it might've stolen this idea from Apple because after all, the Mac Lisa came out way before even Windows one let alone windows 95 or the later version that you might be familiar with. And this even led Apple to Sue Microsoft for infringing on their intellectual rights for using this graphical user interface to interact with the computer. This is how big a deal GUIs were a back in the nineties. There was such a big breakthrough in interacting with computers and that made it so important to both Apple and Microsoft that they ended up battling in court. Now, even to this day, Bill Gates gets asked whether if he actually copied the graphical user interface idea of an operating system from Steve jobs and Apple. But the more colorful piece of history actually comes from the biography of Steve jobs by Walter Isaacson and in there, there is this brilliant depiction of the scene where Steve Jobs, surrounded by his employees, is basically just going off on bill Gates, telling him that you're of ripping us off. I trusted you and now you're stealing from us. You saw the earlier versions of our operating system, and you're now using it in your Microsoft software. And to his credit, Bill Gates actually managed to come up with a pretty good response on the spot where he said, "Well, Steve, I think there's more than one way of looking at it. ### Setting Default Values for Optional Arguments inside a Function Header

In the last lesson, we saw how different it was when we tried to use the turtle's write function and we saw all of the arguments available listed, versus when we tried to use the Tkinter label's pack method, and notice how there's actually very few arguments that are listed. And yet, somehow there's all of these parameters that we can change when we look at the documentation, like expand or side. So let's set that side to equal left, and I'm going to delete the rest of the turtle code. And now you can see our label is placed on the left side of our screen. How is it that these parameters, even though they're not listed in the list of properties, how is it that we're able to use them just by typing them in? Well, to understand this, we have to learn a bit more about advanced arguments. Not how to argue better, but how to use advanced Python arguments in order to specify a wider range of inputs. We've already seen how keyword arguments work. For example, here I have a function and I have three keyword arguments, a, b, and c. And when I call the function, I can provide those inputs, a, b, and c in any order I want as long as I've got the keyword in front. So c = 3, a = 1, and b = 2. Now what if when I use this function, it's nine out of ten times, a is going to be equal to 1, b is 2 and c as 3. Why is it that when I call the function, I always have to put in these values? That seems a bit of a wasted effort, right? Python has a very neat way of solving this by creating arguments that have default values. We can do this by simply changing the function declaration. So when we create our function, we can already give it some values to start off with. So we can say that a should be equal to 1, b = 2 and c = 3, and these are the default values. So that means when I call this function and I want to use the default values, I don't actually have to provide any inputs and it will just go along as it would before. Now, if, however, I wanted to modify one of those inputs, let's say I wanted to give a custom value for b rather than let it be equal to the default value of 2, well, then I can just change the value of b, b = 5. And the rest, so a and c, will still take on their default values. Notice when I called tim.write, this write method takes five inputs; self, because it's a method and associated with the turtle class, it takes an argument which is what it is going to write, move, align and font. Now, if I wanted to use tim.turtle to just write some sort of text, I can actually just put in this. And when I run this code, you'll see that I've got some piece of text being written. But how is it that I've got all of these other inputs which I've just basically completely ignored? What about move? What about align? What about fonts? Well, as you can see, they have the =..., which is trying to tell you that they've already got a default value. And in fact, if I hover over this write function, you can see that in the quick docs that pops up, it tells me that the argument, or the arg, which is what it is to be written to the screen, move which is optional which can be set as true or false, align which is optional, font which is optional. The reason why they're optional is because all of these actually have a default value. For example, move, by default, is false; align by default is centered, and there's also a default font. So that means that all we have to do is just to provide the required arguments. If I don't add anything at all when I call this write method, you can see I do in fact get an error here. And it says write is missing one required positional argument, which is that first arg which is the thing that it's expecting to write. I mean, if you're calling turtle to do some writing and you not telling it what to write, that's a bit of a problem. So this ARG is a required argument because it doesn't have that =... at the end. So this you have to provide. But once you've done that, then the rest of them all have default values. They already know how to behave and what to do even if you don't tell them anything extra. Now, however, if you wanted to modify one of those arguments, let's say I decide to change the font to something completely different like Times New Roman, and make the font super large 80 size font and change it to bold, then you can see that that optional setting gets implemented and it's now changed the font and its changed the size and also made it bold. But this was completely optional. And this is all down to creating the function with default values.

### *args: Many Positional Arguments

In the last lesson, we looked at how to provide default values for optional arguments. In this lesson, we'll discuss how to create functions that can take any number of arguments. Let's say that we had a function called add, which adds n1 and n2 and it just returns the sum of those numbers. That's very well and good, but what if I wanted to add more than two numbers? Well, I would have to add n1, n2, n3, n4, but then I would have to add four numbers every single time. So what if I wanted to make this function more flexible and to allow any number of arguments to be used as the input? Well, what I can do is to simply change the code to use this asterix and then the name of my parameter. That name args is by convention what most Python developers will use. And it simply stands for arguments. But you don't have to stick with that naming if you don't want to. But what you do need is that asterix. That's the really important part. What that tells Python is this function add can accept any number of arguments. And once inside the function, you can actually loop through all of the arguments which is going to be in the form of a tuple and you can do whatever it is you want with each of those arguments. Instead of now passing in only two arguments because that was fixed when we created the function, we can now pass in any number of values like four values or seven values, and we can do whatever it is we want with them. Let's try this code out. I'm going to delete the code related to Python turtle, and I'm going to create a new file called playground.py. And we're going to use this playground.py to test out what we've just learned. I want you to have a think about what you just saw in the slides and see if you can create a function called add where you can pass in as many numbers as you want and it will always add together all of the numbers that are being passed into the function as the input, and then return the total sum. Pause the video and see if you can give that a go. All right. So what we want to do is to be able to call this method add, for example down here and pass in any number of values, right? Let's just go with three to begin with. And then we want to receive all of those values inside this function and then add them all together. So we're going to use that asterix trick. So one * and then we can give a name to the arguments that we receive, which normally is just called args. Now that we've got these args, if I actually go ahead and print it out and we go to run and then run and change this to our playground, you can see it's basically just printing out a tuple. And that tuple represents all the inputs that were passed in when this function was called. And in fact, if I do a time check on this args, you can see it is indeed a tuple. Now, once we've got hold of this args tuple, we can actually loop through it. So we can say for n in args, for each of the numbers in that tuple, let's go ahead and print each of them. You can see it's now separated them all out; three, five, and six. So that makes it easy enough for us to create the sum. So let's create a sum which is equal to zero. And then instead of printing out each of the n, we can just add the n to sum, and finally outside the loop we'll return our sum. So now when we print this final results by calling add three, five, six, you can see it's now added three, five, and six, and we can call this method in different ways. We can add more values to it, two and one, and you can see it's now equal to 17. And you can basically keep going because it can take any number of values. This is all done by this asterix keyword. And it basically packs all of these numbers that you've put in as the input into a tuple called whatever it is you want it to be called. So you can call it numbers if you want, or you can stick to the default, which is just args. And then once we've got that args inside the function, we loop through it and we can do whatever we want to each of the values. Now, in addition to looping through it, you can also access them by index because it's a tuple after all. So we can say args at position zero like this. And if I print that out, you'll see that the value is three because the first one is three. So that's why these unlimited arguments using this * args is also known as unlimited positional arguments, because the position of your arguments which you pass into the function matters' a huge deal because if I fetched the one at position one, it will no longer be three, and it'll now be five. So this is a way for us to be able to define a function and specify a unlimited or unspecified number of inputs. In other words, the number of arguments for the function can vary because the asterix operator collects all of the arguments into a tuple. However, what if we wanted to refer to our arguments by name rather than by position? Well, that is exactly what we'll talk about in the next lesson. So I'll see you there.

----------------------------------------

### **kwargs: Many Keyword Arguments

In the last lesson we saw how the asterix operator could be used to provide any number of positional arguments to a function because it collected them into a tuple. In this lesson, we'll take a look at the double asterix operator, and this is going to allow us to work with an arbitrary number of keyword arguments. Let's see this in action. So let's say I create another function called calculate, and this time I'm going to add two asteriks. And in this case, I'm going to call my argument **kwargs or keyword arguments. What we've done now is we've added two asterisks signs in front of this parameter name, and we've now created unlimited keyword arguments. What this allows me to do is I could basically now call this calculate function, I could pass in a keyword argument, for example, add, and let's give it a value, maybe three, and then let's add another keyword argument which I'll call multiply, set that to equal five. And effectively what this has been turned into is these **kwargs, which is basically a dictionary. So if I print these **kwargs, you can see what gets printed is basically a bog-standard dictionary. And in fact, if we do that type check thing again, so type, you can see it is in fact, a dictionary. This dictionary basically represents each of the keyword arguments and their values. So add is now a key and three is now it's value, multiply's the second key and five is its value. What I can do here is I could do the standard way of looping through dictionary. So I could say for key, value in **kwargs .items, and then I can get access to each of the keys and their values as I loop through the dictionary like this. So add three multiplied by five. Alternatively, I can simply use the names of the keys. So I could just simply print my **kwargs and then use the square brackets and then provide the name of the key, so add for example. And that will give me the value which is three as you can see here. Now, what this allows me to do is it basically lets me look through all of the inputs and find the ones that I want and use them to do something. So for example, in this case, it's a calculate function, right? So we could let's say start off with a normal positional argument, so let's call it n and let's pass in that n at the very beginning. So let's say we start out with the number 2, n is now equal to 2, and then the **kwargs is a dictionary of the remainder arguments. Let's say that I wanted to do some calculations. I wanted to say n+= kwargs, and I'm going to get hold of the value under add. And then I'm going to say, n*= the kwargs, and I'm going to get hold of value of multiply. So now when I go ahead and print my n, you can see that what happens is it takes the first value 2 as equal to n, and then n, this 2, is going to be added to the number I wanted to add which is 3. So 2 + 3 is 5, and then it multiplied that 5 by whatever it is I had stored in multiply. So 5 plus 5, and we get 25. This gives us a more flexible way of working with these arguments. And it gives us a way to name the values that we're passing in to this function. Now, coming back to what they've done in the Tkinter module, basically this Tkinter module is actually ported from another technology called TK. And TK actually has a very different syntax from Python. In order for it to work, they basically took all of the Tk commands, like creating a label or packing some sort of item, and took all of the options and turn them into these **kwargs or optional keyword arguments. And that is why when we create a new label from the Tkinter module or when we call the pack method, you can see that it doesn't actually come up with any properties that we can modify other than this **kw, which is the same as our **kwargs. So we could actually create a class like that as well, because this is done at initialization, right? This is done when they're creating that label class. Let's say that we create a class like this which I'll car, and in the init, what I'll include in addition to self is ** kw, or **kwargs, or however you want to spell it. This kw are going to be all of the optional arguments that I'll pass in when I'm initializing a new object from this class. I can say, for example, self. make of the car equals kw. And then from kw, I'm going to get the make. And then I'm going to have self.model which is going to be equal to kw and then model. And of course, all of the spelling matters so make sure you don't make any typos. And then I decide to create my car which is going to be the object created from this class. Now notice how when I open up the parentheses here, you don't actually see any of the properties like make and model show up when I'm initializing. All you see is ** kw, just in the same way as you see it here, **kw. And that of course refers to our optional keyword arguments. Let's add some values. Let's set the make to a Nissan, and lets set the model to a-- let's set it to a GT-R. And now I can use my object just as I would any other object. I can say my_car.model. And when I hit run, you can see I've got GT-R being printed here. And if I decided to print make, you can see it gets hold off the make. Now, what if I didn't actually specify one of these arguments. Notice how it's now actually going to crash. It tells me that keyError model. So when it was initializing this car object, it fell on this line. And it couldn't get hold of a value called model from this kw argument dictionary. In fact, with dictionaries, we can get hold of the values through the square bracket method, but we can also use a function called get. And we use get in a very similar way to the way that we use the square brackets. We just pass in the name of the key and we want to get hold of the value. But the benefit of get is that if this key doesn't exist in the dictionary, then it will just return none and it won't give us an error. So now if I run this code again, you can see that everything works, but my car.model is now equal to none. So this is how we can actually create a class with lots of optional keyword arguments. So we could have a self.color or self.seats. And depending on what it is we want to initialize this car object to, then we can simply go ahead and add whatever it is we want to set as the make and the model or the color and the seats. And in the same way that way using this label class, we can set the text or we can set the font. We can set all of the options or we can leave them as the default values. That should help you understand how this code works a little bit better. And the reason why it works like this is, as I say, mostly because this module was converted from another language and this just happened to be the most efficient way for them to do this. Now with other more Pythonic modules or things that have been created in Python like the turtle module, then you'll see more bog-standard kind of code like what we've been working with. So when we initialize a new turtle, you can see that it has a default shape, it has a visible boolean, and we can set all of those properties that we can see in this prompt. ### Tkinter Layout Managers: pack(), place() and grid()

Now coming back to our main.py our previous program had a label, a button and an entry, and it was relatively simple. So I'm going to head back to this main.py file where we've got only three widgets so that I can show you how we can define the layout and positioning of each of our widgets. Firstly, I've reconfigured the file a little bit. So I've moved the button _clicked function to the top, and I've made sure that each of the pack methods are at the very end of each widget. That way we'll be able to work with it quite easily. Now, as I mentioned before, tkinter has a whole bunch of different layout managers that define how to position each of the widgets in your GUI program. Now there's three that you should know about, pack, place and grid. Now, firstly, we've already seen pack and all that pack does is it basically packs each of the widgets next to each other in a vaguely logical format. And by default, pack will always start from the top and then pack every other widget just below the previous one. As I mentioned, you can change this by adding a side parameter and you can change it to for example, side = left. And if you change this for all of the packs, then it's going to pack everything starting from the left edge of the program like this. And you can change that to bottom or right as well. But the problem with pack is that it's actually quite difficult to specify a precise position. So for example, if you wanted this label to be a little bit up and then this button a little bit down and this entry all the way to the right. It's very, very complicated to do that using pack. And that's why there's not just a single layout manager, but there's lots of others. So let's take a look at the next one, which is called place. Place is all about precise positioning. So when you place something, you can provide a X and Y value. So for example, I can say my label.place, and then I can say, well, the X value should equal 0 and the Y value should equal 0. And this just places that label at the top left corner. Now it's important to remember that if a widget gets created but it doesn't have any layout specified it using pack, place or grid, then it won't be shown as you can see here, we've only got the label showing up. Now that we've placed our label to the top left corner, we can try placing it in somewhere else. So let's move it a little bit along the X axis. So let's say place it on a (100, 0) That moves it to the right a bit more, and if we want to move it down we can change the Y position. So now it's down at the bottom and then the X is 100. Now, remember we've defined the width and height. So the width is 500 pixels, the height is 300 pixels and anywhere along that screen, you can define a X and Y value for a particular widget to place it at that precise position. The downside of place on the other hand is the fact that it is so specific and we have to work out in our head the coordinate and where to put each widget. It simple enough if you've only got three widgets like we have here, but if you have a hundred or fifty, then that becomes quickly a bit of a nightmare to manage the precise coordinates of each widget. So in addition to pack and place, there's also a final layout manager which also happens to be my favorite one, which is the grid. And the grid is a really simple concept. It imagines that your entire program is a grid and you can divide it into any number of columns and rows that you want to. So just as a reminder, the rows are the ones that go along the horizontal and the columns are the ones that go along the vertical. If I remove my place and instead I use my grid, I could say my_label.grid, and then I can provide a column and a row number. So let's say I'm going to put it at the first column and the first row. So then starts from zero so that we could say column = 0, row = 0. And you can see that it gets placed in the top left corner. Now the grid system is relative to other components. So even if I change this column to, I dunno, five and the row to five, you can see that it doesn't actually change the layout because there is no widget in column four, three, two or one. So it's still the first one in the grid. So the easiest way of working with the grid is starting with the things that you want it to be at the top left, defining a starting column and rows, zero, zero, and then for the next and subsequent widgets to just keep going through it and define its position on the grid. For example, if I wanted the button to be on column one and row one and then I want my entry which is called input to be on the grid in column two and row two, now if you run this, you can see it's now been laid out along our grid. And this is effectively what it looks like. Our label is in column zero row zero, button in column one row one and entry in column two row two. This is one of the easiest ways of visualizing and creating the layout for your tkinter programs. And it's really flexible and it's really easy to imagine and understand. So this is always my preferred way of working with the layout for tkinter. Just a word of warning though. You can't mix up grid and pack in the same program. So for example, if I wanted my label and my button to be defined by the grid but then I decide to use the pack method for my final entry, then you can see I actually get a error when I run my code. It says, cannot use geometry manager pack which already has slaves managed by grid. So these two are incompatible with each other. You basically have to choose one or the other. And often I will choose grid because it's just more flexible and more easy to understand. So now here comes a challenge for you. I want you to change the code that we've already written so that we end up with this layout. So we've already got a label, a button and an entry. I want you to add a new button and it should be positioned like this. Have a think about how you might solve this challenge using the grid system that you learned about just now. Pause the video and complete the challenge. All right. So the first thing you notice is that the label is still at column zero row zero, button is still at row one column one, but this new button is now at row zero column two. So let's go ahead and create it. Now I'm just going to create a new button and I'm not going to worry about its command or any of that. I'll give it a piece of text just so that we can identify it and I'll call it new button. But then the most important thing is how we lay out this new button. So I'm going to use the grid system and I'm going to give it a column of two because it is zero, one, two, the third column from the left and then row is going to be zero. Now, when I run this code though, you'll notice something a little bit odd. Why is the entry below the button? Because in our example, the entry is actually over on the right of this new button in a new column. By putting this new button in between the old button and the entry, we've actually changed the positioning of that entry on the grid. So we've actually had to move it along into the next column. So to do that, we have to change the grid of our entry instead of having column two, to make it column three, just so that its on the right of this new button. And now when I run it, this has the exact layout that we wanted and we've now learned a little bit about how we can precisely position our widgets in our program using the pack, place, and grid layout managers. The very last thing I want to show you with relation to layout and design of our GUI programs is how to add a little bit of padding around components. The easiest way to add padding is actually to directly modify the widgets. So for example, if I wanted a bit of padding around all of the elements in my window, so basically added around the edge of the window, then I could simply say window.config and I can change the padding in the X axis and the padding in the Y axis, so padx and pady. So now if I run this program as it is, you can see that there's now more space being added around all four edges of our program. Now I can make this a lot more extreme. So let's say I add the padx to be 100 and the pady to be 200, you can see just how much padding we've now added. And this just means that you add more space around your program and it makes things easier to see and looks a little bit nicer. If you want to add padding around a specific widget not just the entire window, then you can do the same with that widget. So we could get hold of my label and again using config to change the padx and the pady. So let's add, maybe I dunno, 50 pixels of padding in the X and in the Y. Now you can see that around that label there's a whole lot of space so that it pushes everything else away and actually makes the entire program window a lot bigger. So this is just a way for you to be able to add space around your widgets so that they're not all crushed together and it helps you with your layout and your design.

## Day 28 - Intermediate - Tkinter, Dynamic Typing and the Pomodoro GUI Application

### Day 28 Goals: what we will make by the end of the day

Hey guys, welcome to day 28 of 100 Days of Code. Today we're going to be building a Pomodora app completely from scratch using tkinter and the knowledge that we gained from yesterday's lessons. Now you've already heard me talk about the Pomodoro technique, this famous book by Francesco Cirillo, Cirillo. This famous technique that helps people time-manage and to get more stuff done. Now, if you didn't hear me talk about it, this is basically a very simple breakdown. Essentially, you figure out the task that you need to do something hard, something that takes a while like writing your next book or coding up a project. And then you want to set your timer to the 25 minutes and then work on the task for 25 minutes. And then after that, you take a short five-minute break. And after you've done four of these Pomodoros, basically four repetition, then you get to take a 15 to 30 minute break. So this basically really effectively utilizes the way that our brain works to take short breaks often and to work for 25 minutes at a time, which helps us with information retention and also keeping up the motivation. This is the program that we're going to be building using tkinter. It's going to be a timer with a tomato on it. And when you click start, it's going to tell you to work for 25 minutes. Then that window can go into the background and while you're writing your code or doing whatever, when the timer's up, it will pop to the very front of the screen above all of the other windows and tell you to take a break. So the first break is for five minutes and you'll notice here, we've already achieved one check mark for our first Pomodoro completed. And once you're done with the break, then it's going to go back to work and it's going to continue until you reach the longer break or until you click reset to stop and reset the timer. Effectively, it's going to help you do these Pomodoros where you have 25-minute work, 5-minute break. You do four of these 25-minute work sessions, and then you get a 20-minute break. So hopefully by creating this program, you're going to increase your productivity and you're going to have your own handy tool to help you achieve more and do more. So this is what we're going to be building. Once you're ready, head over to the next lesson and let's get started.

### Add a Count Down Mechanism

In the last lesson, we completed the user interface for our Pomodoro timer, and we've managed to get all the components that we need onto our graphical user interface. Now, the next step is to actually give it some functionality. I want to be able to create some sort of countdown mechanism that just does something really simple. For example, if it was just able to count down from five, four, three, two, one going down by one each time, that would be great. That's what we're going to be working on in this lesson. And we're going to go and see the countdown mechanism section to do that. One of the ways that you might think about approaching this is to use our time module cause we've seen before that we can say time.sleep and we can tell it to sleep for a second. So then we could maybe set up a while loop and while something or other is true, go ahead and sleep for one second. And then afterwards just, you know, subtract one from some sort of counter. So that we could start count at five and then each time we subtract by one and then each time we just simply update our label here, which we created in the canvas to whatever value count might be. Now, that sounds great in principle. The only problem is that we're working within a graphical user interface program. The reason why that's relevant is because if we think about a command line program, say for example, if we were to get our console to do something, print hello, well, it's only going to do something when you actually give it an instruction and you hit enter. It doesn't really need to keep an eye out for what you might do in between. But a graphical user interface is a little bit different. It needs to keep watching the screen to see whether if a user clicks on a button, for example. So it's basically going to refresh and keep listening for events. So every fraction of a second, it's going to keep checking, did something happene, did something happen, did something happen. And the moment when it does, then it's got to react. It's got to react to that event. In this case, we tend to call these types of GUI programs event-driven. And the way that it's driven is through our main loop. So when we set up our window and we start off the main loop, it's basically looping through and every millisecond it's checking to see did something happen, did something happen, did something happen? So that means if we have another loop in our program, it actually won't be able to reach the main loop. And in this case, when you actually try to run it, nothing happens. Our program doesn't even launch. So we have to rethink this and we have to do it a little bit differently. In order to create interactive and interesting programs, you kind of need something to happen on screen, right? Every so often. You need this timing mechanism. Luckily, tkinter already thought of this. And we can in fact use one of the builtin methods to every widget. So if we tap into our window widget, we can get hold of a method called after and after is quite simple. It's a method that takes an amount of time that it should wait and then after that amount of time, it simply calls a particular function that you tell it to call passing in any arguments that you want to give it. Here's how it works. We call window.after, we first provide the amount of time to wait in milliseconds. So if we want one second, then that's 1000 milliseconds. Next we pass in a function to call. So let's create a function up here. Let's just call it, say something, and then we'll pass in the thing, like this. And then all we do is we just print that thing. So super simple function. And then we give the name of this function as the function to call after 1000 milliseconds. Now the final thing in this list of arguments, if I just go ahead and cut that and show you again, when it gives me the prompt, the last thing is actually a *args. This, if you remember, allows us to put in an unlimited number of positional arguments. What that means is we can give as many arguments as we want and those arguments, in this case, is simply going to be passed to the function that we want to call. So in this case, it's going to be that thing. So if I put hello here then I run my code, you can see that after 1000 milliseconds, basically one second, it calls this function, say_something, and it passes this hello as the input to that function. As I said, you can have an infinite amount of positional arguments. So let's put in some other arguments which we'll call a, b, and c, and then we'll print a, print b, and print c. And now instead of passing in hello, we're going to pass in lots of positional parameters. So we'll say 3, 5, and 8. Now, when I hit run, you will see it waits for one second and then it passes all three of these parameters to say something and it goes ahead and prints all of those out at once. So this is how the after method works. But what we wanted to do though, is we want it to repeat itself, to essentially loop. One way of getting that behavior is to simply put this method, call somewhere inside a function and then call itself. So here's what I mean. Let's create a function called a count_down, and this is going to take a input in the form of the number to count down by. And then inside this function, we call window.after. And we say that after 1000 milliseconds, call this function count_down and then pass in a count number. If that count number started out as 5, then we want to say count - 1. Now all we have to do is to call this countdown method. So let's call count_down and passing the starting count, let's say 5 seconds. So now when I run the code, it's going to call this method passing in 5 over here, and then it's going to wait for one second, and then it's going to call this function count_down passing in five minus one so it becomes four. And then afterward it repeats again, becomes three, two, one. So now if we catch that number which we can print, then we'll be able to see it count down when we run the code; five, four, three, two, one. ### Dynamic Typing Explained

In the last lesson, we managed to get our countdown mechanism to work, and we got it to count down from five minutes to zero. Now, everything works, but there's just something a little bit niggling and you'll see it when I hit start. Notice how it says 5:0. Wouldn't it be so much better if it said 5:00? So how would we do that? Well, that is the zero comes from this count_sec because it's taking the count in seconds, dividing it by 60 and finding the remainder using the modulo. Now, when there is no remainder, it's just going to be equal to zero. So we could use an if statement and check well if the count_sec is equal to zero, then instead of making it zero, let's set it to equal a string which is "00". Now this actually, believe it or not, works. And you'll see it when I run it. When I hit start, doesn't that look so much better? But some of you might've realized that there's something a little bit crazy going on here in these two lines of code. We're checking to see if this variable holds data that is equal to the integer, the whole number zero, and then we're setting it to a string. So these are completely two different data types. That's an int and that is a string. So how is it that we're able to do this? So let me pull up the Python console. We know that if we took a integer, say 3, and we try to add it to a string, say a 4, this is not going to work and we get a type error because this is type int and this is type string. So you can't actually add these two together because there's a mismatch. Now here's the crazy thing. Let's create a variable a and let's make it hold the integer with 3. And at this point, you can see that this a variable has a data type of int. If I decide to change that variable and make it hold a different type of data, let's say the number 4, or let's make it simpler, let's make it hold the piece of text, Hello. As soon as that goes through, you can see that a is now of data type string. And the very fact that I'm able to do that, change a variable's data type by changing the content in that variable, this is what's known as dynamic typing. In this sense, Python is a language that's quite unique because on one hand it is strongly typed, in the sense that it holds on to the data type of the variable, so this a is a string and it knows that it's a string and if you do something that is not meant for a string, say if you try to raise a to the power of 2, then that is going to be a type error. Types matter and when you call a function that's expecting a particular type, say if you use the power function which is expecting a integer and you pass in something that's obviously not an integer say, our string here and you try to get it to do some things, say raise it to the power of 3, then again, we get type error. It knows what type is supposed to go into that function and it makes sure that you comply with that. This is where the language is strongly typed. But the part where the language is dynamically typed is that even though it knows what type a variable is, it knows what type a function expects, you can also dynamically change the data type of any variable like this. That is basically what we're using here. We're using dynamic typing to change the data type of count_sec from a integer to a string. And then we use that string to display inside this canvas text. Now there is however, still a bit of a bug with this and you'll see it once it dips below 10 seconds. Notice that as soon as it goes to 9 seconds, instead of saying 09, which is what you would want or 08, 06, it just lists the number of seconds until it reaches 00. So how can we fix this? The key lies in these two lines of code. See if you can do this as a challenge, pause the video and see if you can make it so that when it's nine seconds remaining, it says 09 or 08 or 07 and also 00 of course. Pause the video and see if you can complete this challenge. All right. So basically what we want to check for is when the count in seconds is less than 10, because now it's going to be in the single digits and instead of having just one digit, we wanna add a zero in front of it. So the way we can do this is through just an f-string. We can use an f-string to add the zero in front and then add the count in seconds afterwards, formatting that into the standard kind of time format. Now that we fixed that if we run our app again it goes down to 10 seconds you can see it now says 09, 08, 07 and it's nicely formatted using our f-string. And we're able to do because of the flexibility of the data types in Python, checking it as a number, making sure it's less than 10 and then formatting it as a string and using the f-string. Now, this is not a feature that's available in all programming languages. For example, languages like C or Java or Swift, you won't be able to do this. Once you create a variable and you give it a certain type of data, then it must forever hold on to that type of data. But Python allows you to change the data type of a variable just by assigning it to a different type of value. There's a really well-worded Stack Overflow answer that addresses this exact thing I'm talking about, talking about the fact that Python is a strongly dynamically typed language. And I recommend that if you want to dig more into this, to have a read of this answer and I'll link to this in the course resources.

### Challenge 2 - Use grid() and columnspan to Complete the User Interface

To go from this, to this will require not only some widgets to be added but a little bit more knowledge about how to lay out our widgets on the grid. Because notice how here we've got a single entry that is spread across the right side of the screen, but then down here we've got an entry that's only taking up a part of that space. Effectively, if we think about our grid, this particular entry is actually taking up two columns. So how can we do this? To demonstrate this, I've created a sandbox app. So it's super simple, all it has is a red label and a green label. And you can see that the red label has a width of 20, and a height of 5, as does the green, but the red is on row=0, column=0, whereas the green is on row=1, column=1. So we get this kind of checkered kind of look. If I decide to go and add another label, let's call it 'b' for blue, and I give it a background of blue, and then I give it the same width and height. Now if I put this new label onto the grid and I put it on to the next row, so row= 2, but the column I'm going to put it on column=0. Now, I think at this point you can probably all predict where that label is going to go. And indeed it goes on to the very first leftmost column and it's on the third row. Now, what if I wanted that blue label to go across the entire width so that it's below the red and also below the green. Well, you might think that I could simply just double the width, right? Instead of a width of 20, let's change it to 40. Surely, that's going to stretch this label so that it goes across the entire red and green label. But unfortunately, when I run this, you'll see, instead, this happens. The blue label is still within the first column, and in fact, it's stretched that column to a 40 width, and that red column is now centered again in the leftmost or the first column, and that blue is nowhere near the green label, because it's not allowed to go into that second column. So how can we solve this situation? Well, the actual answer is another attribute that the grid has, which is something called a columnspan . Now the columnspan is exactly what it sounds like, really, it's basically how many columns is this particular thing going to span. So in our case, we want it to go across two columns column 0 and column 1. So it should start out at column 0 but then span a whole 2 columns, and now when I run this code you can see we get our desired effect. The blue label is now across the red and the green and it's spanning two columns. The link to this playground is in the Course Resources, so feel free to head over there and give it a go if you want to play around with this example. Now, in our case, if we break down the final layout we're looking for, it's effectively a three-column, and five-row layout. So we've already got our canvas which is actually going to go in the middle, so probably the second column. And then we've got the Website, the Email/Username, the Password, and finally our two Buttons. Now I've laid out this entire user interface, and I've specified the width of some of these entries and buttons, just because you'll need to do a bit of tweaking around just to make sure that everything lines up with each other. I've already done that ahead of time, and I've really worked out the sort of near optimal width. So what I want you to do is to use what we've learned about the Grid Columnspan, so if we have our Label, our Button, New Button, and Entry, if I want this particular button to go across two columns, then I have to change that columnspan attribute to 2. ### Dialog Boxes and Pop-Ups in Tkinter

Now in the last lesson, we managed to get our password manager to start saving the data that we're entering inside the password manager. And we formatted it and put it inside our data.txt. Now, one of the things that was a bit of an issue in terms of user experience is whenever the user actually enters their details into this password manager at the moment, it doesn't actually give you some sort of way of knowing that it was successful or if it was not, or actually getting them to check and verify that the data that they've entered is definitely the one that they want to save into the file. In order to do this, we're going to learn about something else that you can do with tkinter which is something called standard dialogs. These are basically popups that your tkinter program can generate. And one of the most popular standard dialogs are the message boxes. And it's really, really easy to create these popups. You can simply just import the message box module and you can tap into methods like show info or show warning, show error, or you can ask the user yes no, or OK or cancel, ask a question yes or no, ask to retry or cancel. Now the screenshots where made in a Swedish version of Windows, but we can actually try these out ourselves and start putting in some standard dialogs so that we can give the user some feedback. The thing that we really want to tell the user is the moment that the save function is called it's because they pressed on the add button here. So we can create a message box here and get them to check the details that they've entered and then hit yes or no as to whether if they want to save it. Now notice how this is not actually a class. The thing that's important though is to actually put it into use. So we can use the message box and call a method to show a popup. So we have to plan for these eventualities just as, you know, your car is probably not going to break down, but you need breakdown cover just in case that it does happen. In programming what we can do is we can catch these exceptions. When something goes wrong and in that moment we catch that exception, then it doesn't have to fail catastrophically. We have try, except, else and finally. These are the four keywords that are really important when it comes to handling exceptions. In most cases, it probably will work, but sometimes it just might not. Now the next step is to define the except block. So this is the block of code that you want the computer to execute if there were more was an exception. If something went catastrophically wrong and it was not the way that you expected it to go, then carry out this piece of code. Now the else keyword allows you to find some code to execute if there were no exceptions. If you tried this thing that might fail but actually it didn't fail. You succeeded and there were no problems. Well then, in this case, you're going to do whatever is inside the else block. And then finally, we have the finally keyword which basically is just the block of code to carry out no matter what happens. If this thing that you tried failed or if it succeeded, Honeybadger, I mean, finally doesn't actually care. So no matter what happens with trying this line of code, this finally block is always going to be executed and it's usually used for cleaning things up or tidying things up at the end of some sort of code execution. ### Raising your own Exceptions

In this lesson, I'll show you how you can generate your own exceptions in case your code encounters unexpected situations. So these are the four keywords are most important when it comes to error handling and catching exceptions. The final keyword that is related is one called raise. Now, when I hit run you can see no matter what happened, and in fact, there is no error. I decided to raise this error and that's what I see right here. I could change that to a type error, and that is what will crash my code. And I can even specify a message along with this error. So I could say raise a type error and let's just say the message is, and you can see now when it runs, it hits that type error. And it says, this is an error that I made up. So when might you want to raise errors? Well, let's comment out all the code that we have because we have that type error at the end so it's always going to crash the code no matter what. So let's comment it out and let's start from scratch. Let's say that I decided to calculate the body mass index or the BMI of somebody's and I'm getting them to input their height as a float. No matter which way we use, we can print out the BMI. ### Write, read and update JSON data in the Password Manager

The goal is to take our password manager to the next level. And in order to do that, we need to add a search functionality. It's not good enough just to look through the data file anymore. What we want to be able to do is to type a website into the website entry, and then hit search, and we get a pop up showing us our email and the password that was saved for that website. So this is the goal. But where we're currently at is we have a text file which contains the name of the website, the email and the password. This is very difficult to search and this is a really terrible format to work with. So we're going to be levelling up our data storage in our password manager. And we're going to switch from saving data straight to a text file to a fancier data format, which is called JSON. Nope. This is not the latest, hottest DJ on the block. Lock. It's actually JSON, which stands for JavaScript Object Notation. This was something that was designed originally for JavaScript, but because it has such a simple structure and it's so easy to understand and work with that it's been adopted by many, many different fields, including Python. This is probably one of the most popular ways of transferring data, especially when you're transferring data across the internet. So this is what we're going to be learning about. And for those of you looking at this slide, you might have already realized that it's kind of similar to the dictionaries that we've been working with in Python. Right? A JSON is essentially composed of a bunch of nested lists and dictionaries, and it has that key value pair data structure. This is essentially what we're aiming for, so that we can store our data in this format. And we'll be able to easily load up this data and search through it for the particular website that we want the information for. To work with JSON data in Python, we can use the inbuilt JSON library, and we're going to use it to write, read and update data to a JSON file. To begin, I'm going to simplify our code a little bit. I'm going to get rid of this message box which asks the user okay or cancel. We're just going to assume that once they click add, then they're happy with the email and password. So now that we've cut down that little bit of code, it makes this a little bit easier to understand. All that we're doing here is we're checking to make sure that the length of the website entry and the length of the password entry is equal to zero. ### Solution & Walkthrough for Flipping Cards

Now that we've got our words showing up in French, it's time to see the other side of the card and see the English equivalent so that we can check our knowledge. To do this we're going to have to implement some sort of way of changing this card after a set amount of time. So we're going to flip the card after three seconds are up. To do that we're going to use the window.after method. Right after here where we've created a window, we're going to say window.after. And then we can specify the amount of time in milliseconds. So I'm going to say three seconds or 3000 milliseconds. And then the function that we're going to call is a function that's going to be called flip_card. And if we want that to work, then we're going to have to create it. So I'm going to create right here, just above. So I'll call it flip_card and this function is going to take care of changing the card to show the English word for the current card, and also going to change the image from the card_front to the card_back, and also we're going to change the color of the text as well. In our flip card, we're going to get hold of the canvas and we're going to first item.config the card_ title. So we're going to change the card_title to, instead of saying French, we're going to say, well, this is now the English translation, and then we're going to config the card word, and this is going to be still from the current card, but we want to get ahold of the value under the key English instead. Now at the moment, this current card is locked up inside next_card. So we can't actually get hold of it without creating a new random choice. So what we can do is we can create our current card and we can set it to a empty dictionary. And then we can change this to a global and tap into that current card to modify it and save this random choice from our list of French and English pairs. So once we've got that inside there, then we can tap into it inside flip_card and we can say current card get hold of the value under the English key. And that way we update both of our texts. So right now if I hit run, you can see that immediately after three seconds we switched to the opposite side and we have our English and the English equivalent of the same word showing up. So for example, in French matin, in English means morning. So that's how we can verify that we actually know the meaning of the card. In addition to changing the words, I'm also going to change the image. So notice how we saved the words with a variable. We can do the same thing for this create image method. We can say the card_background is equal to canvas create image. And in addition to creating the card front image, we can also create the card back image. Now, you have to be really careful here because if you create this card back image which is a photo image created from file, if you create it inside one of these functions, by the end of the function call, that reference to that particular image will be gone. And it won't work if you create this photo image inside flipcard and try to set it inside this method. So you have to create it outside of any of the functions. So let's change the file to images/card_back.png and now we're going to get our canvas to again, call itemconfig. And this time we're configuring the card_background. And the attribute that we want to configure is the image property. So we're going to change that to the card_back_img which we created right here. So now let's just check that again. Let's wait three seconds and then it's changed to the back of the card. On the back of the card we want these two pieces of text to actually have a different color. We want it to be white, just so that it stands out from the background. And to do that, we can add it along with our item config. Not only are we changing the text, but also changing the fill of the text to white. Okay. And now when our card flips over, you can see its a green card with a white text. Now, one of the things we have to do is every time we click on one of these buttons, it has the flip back to the front of the card, right? That means changing the text color and changing that background image. So that happens when we go to next card. So in addition to configuring the text and the words, we also again have to itemconfig the card_background so that we can change the image back to the card front image. In addition, we have to change these text colors to have a different fill, so we're going to change it back to black. Right. This way, when the card flips, it goes to green, white on green. And then when we go to the front of the card, it goes to black on white. Now notice how once we go to the next card, that card flipping mechanism has gone because we only ever call this window after the first time we create the window. So we actually need this to happen a few times. In fact, we need it to happen every single time we go to the next card. So after we've configured all the things on our card, we're gonna call a window.after, three seconds, flipcard. So this way, even if we go to the next card and we wait three seconds, it again goes to the back. Now one of the bugs you might have encountered is if you clicked this button many times and you go through lots of different words, you see immediately, that card actually flipped. And it's because that window.after three seconds is counting down in the background, waiting, waiting, waiting until three seconds at which point it's going to flip the card. It doesn't care that you've actually just gone onto a new card and you want to wait again, three seconds. In order to get this to work, we actually have to give this line of code a variable so that we'll call it the flip_timer. And this is now a global which we can tap into and we can add it after a comma over here, flip_timer. Alternatively, you can also go onto a new line and say global flip_timer. It doesn't really make a difference other than the fact that this probably takes less lines of code. Now, once we've got access to our flip_timer, we can say that every time we go to a new card, when we click on one of these buttons, we're going to invalidate this timer. So we can say window.after_ cancel and then pass in the ID of our flip_timer. And then after we've set up this card, we can set up a new flip_timer so that it waits for again three seconds. And now once I've added that bit of code, it should fix this bug. So now whenever I keep going or I press the check or the crossmark, it doesn't really matter. It's not going to flip until I land on a card and wait for three seconds before it flips. There you have it. We've got our card flipping technology added to our code. Now, in addition to saving it to CSV, we also have to read from that CSV because instead of using the words from our original list which is our french_words.csv, I actually want to be able to read from my words_to_learn.csv instead, because that way, every single time I rerun the app, it's always going to give me all the words that I've yet to learn. So currently we're on 87. If I run this again, you can see that the first time I click on this, it's going to go to 86 instead of going back to 100. But there is a problem here though because if I delete this file, words_to_learn.csv, and I go ahead and run this, the first time this runs it's going to crash and we have that familiar file not found error. So we know how to deal with that. We need to catch this exception. The exception occurs right here. It happens when we try to get hold of this piece of data which may or may not exist. So if it does not exist, so we're going to catch this except file not found error. Well, in that case, we're going to be using the original data which comes from the french_words.csv. So we'll say pandas. read_csv and then we're going to read this file, data/french_words.csv. So this is always going to be there because it's preloaded with our project. But if we do manage to find our words_to_learn.csv, then that means this program has been run before and we've removed some of the words we already know. So we can catch that with an else statement and we can say, well, in this case, we're going to set a global variable called to_learn which starts out as an empty dictionary. And we set it to the data that comes from this CSV. However, if that file was not found, then this to_learn is going to be set to the original data.to_dict and we're going to orient according to records as well. Okay. Now, when we run our code, you can see we have no errors. And the first time that it runs, it's going to pick from our french_words.csv. So if I run this code again, you can see now I have three columns of all of the records. So basically when we read from this particular CSV, we generate a data frame. And when I read from that data frame, so let's delete this and run our code again, you can see that pandas is automatically added in these record numbers. So that gets then added back into our words_to_learn.csv when it saves it into the file. If we want to get rid of these record numbers, all we have to do is when we save it to the CSV, we can set a property called index to false. This way it just doesn't add the index numbers to our newly created list and now if I rerun this code, you can see that our words_to_learn.csv doesn't actually include an index. It only includes the actual records or the actual words and their English translations. That's basically it. That's all the solutions to our capstone project. ### How to Send Emails with Python using SMTP

The first thing we have to figure out is how exactly does email work? We all know that we can log onto Gmail or yahoo.com and we can start filling out an email. It's pretty much second nature to everybody by now. But what actually happens behind the scenes? Well, let's say that we have a sender, angela@gmail.com and a recipient, timmy@yahoo.com. Now, in order to send this email from my Gmail account to another email account, what happens behind the scene is that there's a Gmail mail server, which will receive my message. And then there's a Yahoo Mail server, which will store the message until Timmy logs onto his computer and logs onto yahoo.com, which downloads the email from the Yahoo Mail server. So this email is going to move between all of these steps. And in order to do this, it relies on something called SMTP, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. And this contains all of the rules that determine how an email is received by mail servers passed onto the next mail server and how email can be sent around the Internet. Now, a good analogy for SMTP is if you imagine these mail servers as a post office and Timmy's computer being the mailbox. Then SMTP is basically the postman who knows how to handle the email and take it to various post offices and eventually put it into Timmy's computer. So in Python there's a module called smtplib, which allows us to use SMTP to send our email to any address on the Internet. To start, I recommend setting up two fresh email accounts. Create a new email account with Gmail and also create a new email account with Yahoo. These new email accounts will be perfect for testing your code and following along with the video tutorials. Plus, we'll be making those email accounts a little bit less secure to test our code. So that's another reason to set up some testing email addresses for now. After you've set up your new email accounts, head over to the Course Resources and download the zip file with the starting code for today's lessons. And then we're going to open that up using PyCharm. Now I want you to take a look inside the starting project. There is a main.py file and there's also a quotes.txt file. Don't worry about this file for now, we're going to come back to it when we explore the datetime module. For now, we're going to be working within the main.py. And I want to show you how you can use this smtplib library to start sending emails straight from your Python code. As always, we import the module smtplib and then we can start using it. Once we've imported this SMTP library essentially, we can use it to create a new SMTP object. So we're going to call that object a new connection because it's basically a way for us to be able to connect to our email provider's SMTP email server. We're going to do this by tapping into the smtplib and then creating an object from the SMTP class. Now, when we create this object, one of the things that we should specify is the location of our email providers SMTP server. Now for Gmail, it's simply smtp.gmail.com, but it's different for every email provider. So that means if your email ends in @gmail.com, then this would be how you would connect to your email server. In our case, I've created a testing email called appbreweryinfo@gmail.com. And this part that's before the @ sign is the identity of my email account. And the part after the @ sign is the identity of my email provider. So in my case, I need to connect to smtp.gmail.com. But if you have a different email provider, for example if you're with Hotmail, it's smtp.live.com, and if you are with Yahoo, it's smtp.mail.yahoo.com. And if you're with a completely different email provider than simply just Google your email provider and the SMTP information, and you should find an article somewhere that describes a URL that looks something like this. Once I've created my connection, the next thing I need to do is to go ahead and call starttls(). Now, TLS stands for Transport Layer Security, and it's a way of securing our connection to our email server. So that way when we're sending an email, if somebody else intercepts our email somewhere along the line and they try to read it, because this is enabled that message will be encrypted and it'll be impossible for them to read what is in the content of our email. So this line basically will make this connection secure. Now, once we've secured our connection, the next thing to do is to actually log in. So we'll call connection.login() and here we have to provide a username and a password. So the username is simply the email that we use to log on to our email service. So in my case, it's just my_email and the password, I've just made up a new password. So my made-up password is ABCD1234 and then two brackets. And once I've logged in to my email provider, the final thing I want to do is to actually send my mail. And make sure that you haven't got any typos in your email, your password, the SMTP URL or the recipient email address. Now finally, the last thing we want to add is the message. So this is what we actually want to send in our email. And just like we did with our file when we opened it at the very end, once we're done with it we're going to close it off as well.
