### Python Functions as First Class Objects: Passing & Nesting Functions

The next part of the syntax that might be unfamiliar is this @ sign and something that comes after the @ sign. Now we sort of know what it does. It's basically saying when the user hits up this path which is what's called the home route, basically when you go to a website, for example, www.google.com and you go to the first forward slash well, that is going to be the home. And it knows that when you go there you want to see the home page. So that's effectively what we're saying here. When the user navigates to our URL with just a forward slash they want to see the homepage and so we're going to show them hello world. But what is this syntax exactly? Well, this is code a Python decorator and this is something that you'll see in more advanced Python projects. So what exactly is a decorator? Well, let's imagine that you have a bunch of functions in your class or in your module and you want to add some functionality to each of these functions. Well then you might use a decorator function to do that. Essentially you can think of a decorator function as a function that's going to give additional functionality to an existing function. In order to really understand this, we have to understand a couple of other concepts as well. So I'm going to do a couple of demos in this Repl.it and if you head to this URL or find it in the course resources, you'll be able to see all the code that I've written in this file. So a long time ago, we learned about Python functions and we know that a function allows us to have specific packages of functionality, allows us to add inputs, to increase the reusability of the function, and also allows us to get outputs from the function which we can pass into another function or do something with it. As an example, we've got four very simple functions, add, subtract, multiply, and divide that uses all three components of a function. Now, what if we wanted to get a little bit fancier? Well, one of the things about Python functions is that they are known as first-class objects, which basically means that you can pass a function around as an argument, just like what you could do with an integer, a string or a float, it's treated identically. That means we can take these functions and we can build another function that uses these functions. Let's say I create a calculate function which takes a calc_function and then the n1 and n2. Inside this calculate function, I'm going to call the function that was passed in and give it the values n1 and n2 that was also passed in. So now when I call the calculate function, I'm going to pass in the name of one of these functions and then some numbers. Those numbers are gonna become the input for this specified function and then we're going to return the result of that calculation. So now lower down, I can call my calculate function, pass in the name of a function so for example our multiply function, and then pass in some numbers, for example, two and three. Now let the output that's returned be our results and let's go ahead and print this result. And you can see we get six. So basically it has now multiplied two by three. Now, if I change this to one of the other functions, add, and I run this again, you can see instead of six, I'm now getting five. The ability for us to treat functions as first-class objects basically means that we can pass them around as if they were just any other argument like a number or a string or a floating point number. And then later we can activate them by adding the brackets around them and then any necessary inputs. Now, the next concept which you might've come across but we haven't really used it a lot is the concept of nested functions. Functions can also be nested inside other functions. For example, if I create a function called outer_function and this function is just going to print and say, I'm outer. Now inside this outer_function, I could create another function. So notice the indentation here means that this function is now created inside this function and I'll call it the nested_function. So this function is simply going to print I'm inner. And now we have the problem of trying to call this function. Now, because this function was declared inside this function, its scope means that it's only accessible inside the confines of this function. So if we were to go outside of the function, so by indenting back to the beginning and we try to call this nested function, then it's actually not going to work. We're going to get a name error. It's not defined. However, if we call this function inside this outer_function, then it will now no longer generate an error. So let's go ahead and trigger the outer_function by calling it in our main. py. And when I run this, you can see it says I'm outer and then it says I'm inner. So this first gets executed and then this. And this I'm inner is being printed when this line is being evaluated. Now, one of the other things you could do is you can actually return a function from another function. Right. Functions can actually be returned from other functions. So if I make a copy of this previous function right here and comment out this other function and all the steps before, ... and we only have this bit of active code, then you can see that instead of calling this nested_function here, I could also return it as the output. But the important part here is I'm going to get rid of the parentheses which means I'm no longer activating that function right here. So now when I call this outer_function, the output that this line is going to evaluate to is going to become the nested_ function. So you could almost store it inside a variable. So let's say I create a variable called inner_function which is equal to the output of the outer_function which is basically this nested_function that's being returned. Well then, not only can I trigger the outer_function which is just going to give me I'm outer, now I can also trigger the inner_function separately by calling it and then adding the activator which is the parentheses. So now it says I'm outer after it evaluates this line, I'm inner after it evaluates this line. Now, if this is confusing to you, I recommend heading over to the course resources where I've got a link to this Python Tutor where I've entered all the code that we've seen just now and we can execute this code line by line. So you can see that the first thing that happens is it looks at this outer_ function and it creates a reference to that function. Now next, it's on this line where our outer_function is actually being executed because it has the parentheses at the end. So now it's actually going to go inside this outer function and go through it line by line where it prints I'm outer and then sets up a reference to this second function, which is the nested_function. The nested_function can now be called by its name which is nested_function. But the very end of the outer_function, that function is going to be the return value. So it's going to be outputted. Finally, we get to the end of this line nine and we set up a reference from this variable called inner_function to this nested_function. And finally, when we get to the line 10 we trigger that function. So here is our inner_function which points to this nested function and so when we trigger this inner_function, it's the same as triggering the nested_function. And that is when we end up going into this function and printing out what it says inside. Have a play around with that to fully get to grips with all the things that you can do with a function. And once you're happy with all of this and you've reviewed it and you understand everything that's going on, then you've got the foundations to head over to the next lesson where we're going to talk about Python decorators.

### Understanding Python Decorator Functions and the @ Syntax

In the last lesson, we had a primer on functions so that we can understand the next step which is the Python decorator. So we've seen that functions can have functionality, inputs, and outputs, functions are first-class objects and can be passed around as arguments, functions can be nested in other functions, and finally, functions can be returned as the output from another function without needing to trigger it. With these four things in mind, we're finally ready to tackle the Python decorator. First of all, I'm actually going to create a Python decorator for you so that we can talk about how it works. Here's what a Python decorator function looks like. We started off by creating just a normal function. Let's say I call it my decorator_function. This function is going to take another function as an input. Now, inside the decorator_functionn, I'm going to nest a wrapper_function. And this wrapper_function is then going to trigger the actual function that was passed in to the decorator function. And at the end of calling all the lines in my decorator_function, I'm going to return my wrapper_function. But remember without the parentheses. Now, basically what we've done is we've created a decorator_function which can do some stuff and it could control the calling of the function that was passed in. Remember that a decorator_function is just a function that wraps another function and gives that function some additional functionality. That's quite a mouthful, but let's take a look at an example. Let's say that I wanted to create a simple function which I'll call say_hello. Now this function is going to be the simplest form of function. It has no inputs and it has no outputs and all it does is just going to print hello. Now, what if I don't want to run this immediately the moment when I hit run, what if I wanted to add a delay to this function? Well, one way of doing that would be importing the time module and then before we print hello, we can go ahead and run time.sleep and we can sleep for a prespecified number of seconds. So now when I call this method, say_hello, and when I run it, you'll see that immediately nothing happens. And then after a two second delay, you can see the print hello actually gets triggered. Now, what if I wanted to create a whole bunch of functions like say_bye and say_greeting. And I wanted to add a delay onto each of these. Well, then I would have to copy and paste this code into all three places. No, we definitely saved it. What's actually happening is that to save your internet usage, Chrome likes to cache the style sheets and other static files, so images or JavaScript. and the reason why it does that is because when you visit a website, if you're visiting it on the same day, these static files are unlikely to change. A website is unlikely to update their CSS or their images over one day. So once the browser downloads it, it keeps hold of those static files. This just means that you don't have to keep downloading these large files every single time you hit up the same website. That's kind of good if we are in fact visiting a real live website. But when we're testing, it's a little bit confusing. So one of the things you have to do is you have to get Chrome to hard reload. And you can do that by holding down the shift key and clicking on this refresh button, which is going to do a hard reload. And it's going to get rid of all the cached files and pull in any new files. So now the background changes to red. And we can confirm that by... let's change this to blue hit save on that file, holding down shift, reload, and we get the blue background updating. So that's just something to be careful about when you find that your CSS files or your other static files are not being changed or not being rendered.

## Day 57 - Intermediate+ Templating with Jinja in Flask Applications

### Day 57 Goals: what you will make by the end of the day

Hey guys, welcome to day 57 of 100 Days of Code. Today we're going to be digging deeper into building more advanced Flask applications. And in order to do that, we're going to be learning about URL building and templating with Jinja. So very often when you're creating a website, you'll get cases where you actually don't want to create the page entirely from scratch. For example, if you had a blog and you wanted to have several different posts in the blog, you don't want to create a separate HTML file for each blog post. So in that case, it's really helpful to have a templating language where you can replace bits of that blog with dynamic content. And that's where Jinja comes in. This is a templating language built for Python, and it's going to allow us to create the general layout of our blog, the styling and the structure, and then to replace the content, for example, the title or the subtitle or the body with dynamic content that's generated each time we load a specific page. And by the end of today, you will have built a very simple blog with a number of blog posts. So here we can see the title and subtitle. And then when we click on read to see the blog post in detail, we go to a different page. And depending on which of these blog posts we've clicked on, you can see that we're rendering basically the same layout, the same styling and the same structure, but each time for each of these pages, we're getting some different content. So that's the goal. And once you're ready, head over to the next lesson and we'll get started.

### Using Jinja to Produce Dynamic HTML Pages

Now to begin, all we need is a simple Flask application. You can either write this out from scratch for practice, or you can head over to the course resources and you can download this file as a zip file. Once you've unzipped it and opened it in PyCharm, you should see a server.py file which contains all of the basic code that is required to render hello world onto the screen. So if we go ahead and just run this file and go to the local URL of our website, you should just be able to see hello world. Now, the next thing I want you to do is to create an HTML file which you'll call index, and inside this HTML file, we're going to give it a title of just my website and the more important part is going to occur in the body. For practice, go ahead and see if you can create an h1 that says hello world instead of returning just a hello world as text, and render this index HTML onto the screen instead. Pause the video and see if you can complete this challenge. All right. So the first thing we have to do was to create an h1 that said hello world. And once we've created our index.html, we want to render it as a template instead of just returning this text. So to do that, we're gonna need this render template function at the top. So if we're going to say render template, and then the template we want to render is called index.html. But one thing you have to remember is that this file has to be inside a folder called templates because Flask has specific requirements for things like static files and templates. So now we should be ready to rerun our app so that it will take into account the new files and then go to our website and you should see this hello world is being rendered from our index.html. Now, one of the things you might be wondering is why is this a template? Why are we rendering a template when in fact what we're doing is just sending over an HTML file? Well, the HTML files can actually act as a template as long as we know how to work with a templating language. The templating language that we're going to use is called Jinja and this is specific for Python. It allows us to use some syntax like these curly braces, percentage signs, or double curly braces in order to specify inside the HTML file which parts should actually be evaluated as Python code. Let me show you something. We've already seen that just by putting this text in between the h1 we get this rendered as text in the h1. And if I go ahead and I wrote something like 5 * 6, what would you expect our website to look like? ### Multiline Statements with Jinja

In the previous lessons, we've seen how we can use the Jinja markup in order to insert bits of Python code into the HTML template. Now, in this lesson, I want to demystify some of the other markup like the {% and some of these keywords. Now, what we've been able to do with this markup is to specify single line expressions in Python. But what if we wanted to create multiline statements like an if statement or a for loop? Well, we would have to use some slightly different markup. I'm going to go ahead and create a new HTML file which I'll call blog. And this will have the title of blog and in the body what I want to do is to render all the titles of all the blogs I have. Now in order to get hold of some data for our blogs, we're going to use a service called endpoint. And this is a really neat service which just acts as JSON storage bin. So basically you can create your own API with your own JSON data and you don't even have to log in. It's as simple as clicking on, create JSON bin, and then here you can create some, um, keys, some values or a list of values. And once you've done that, you can go ahead and access this bin at this particular API and you can see it sends you that JSON back. So you can update anything in here and you can get that data coming back to you via this API. That means that I could create some blog posts where each blog post has an ID, a title, a subtitle and body. And I've only got three blog posts in my list. But you can now use this as if it were an API simply by heading to this address, which you'll find in the course resources. Now, what we're going to do is we're going to pull down these blog posts as if it was an API, and we're going to try and display all of the titles and all of the subtitles. Inside our server.py, if we go ahead and set up a new app.route, and this route is going to be /blog, then here we're going to create a blog function which is going to fetch all the blogs from this URL. So I'm going to copy the URL of my API and you can do that in the course resources. And then we're going to put this as the blog URL. Now I'm going to use requests. get to get hold of the data at that URL, and then I can tap into the data by saying response.json and this will give me all of the blog posts. So we'll call that all posts. And now I'm going to render my blog.html and I'm going to pass in all the posts under a keyword called posts... like this. So I've fetched all of those posts, I've passed it into a variable called all_post, and I'm sending that value over to the blog.html under the name posts. So now going to my blog.html, I should be able to catch that post. And if we were just writing Python straightaway, then we would be able to say something like for blog posts in posts, let's go ahead and create an h1 where we have the blog post title, and let's create a h2 where we have the blog post subtitle. And it would, in an ideal world, loop through all the posts it received and for each of the blog posts, render an h1 for the title and h2 for the subtitle. Now, in fact, using Jinja, we can pretty much do exactly this, but we have to alter things a little bit. Firstly, when we have a multiline statement, we're going to have to add a curly brace and then a percentage sign for each of the lines. So not just from the beginning to the end, but for each of the lines that's Python code that spans multi lines we have to enclose it inside this kind of markup. So notice the direction of the curly braces and also notice the presence of the percentage signs. Now inside the part where we insert it into HTML elements, we can do just as we did before, pass through the blog post and render it as a single line expression like this. But because we're working inside an HTML file, we also have to specify when our for loop actually ends. And that very end is also going to be enclosed inside one of these percentage curly brace. And there's a special key word that comes from Jinja which is called endfor in order to specify at the end of the for loop. We'll just have to add it in like this. Now, if we go ahead and hit save, and now if we run our code and try to bring up our blog website, you should see that it's pulled in all of the articles in our fake blog, the life of cactus, top 15 things to do when you're bored, and introduction to intermittent fasting. It's a really random blog that we're starting and it's created an h1 for each of the titles and h2 for each of the subtitles. And it's done this without us having to pass out each of the title, subtitles. We've actually been able to do all of that just with a for loop inside our template. Now you can do the same thing using an if statement. All you have to do is to, again, enclose every line in the statement with {%, and then at the very end of your block of code, of your statement, you have to add the endif keyword as well. See if you can modify this so that we only print out the title for the blog post which has an ID of 2. All right, in this case, all we have to do is add an if statement down here. We're going to say if the blog post that we're currently looping on has an ID that's equal to 2, well, in that case, we actually want to render the title and subtitle, but otherwise, we're not going to. All we have to do is add in the markup. So starting at the first if statement, we add the {% at the beginning and at the end, and at the very end of the if statement we add the {% and that keyword endif to say that this is the end of the if statement. So now if we hit save and we go back to our blog, you can see that it's only going to show the second article, the one with ID of 2.

### URL Building with Flask

So now that we've seen some of the things that we can do with templating and Jinja, I want to talk to you about something called URL building. And this is a way that allows us to direct the user to a specific page in our website and web app. Now, what that means is that for example, on our main homepage, we could actually have a link to the blogs page. The way that we would do that is in our index.html here, we could create a anchor tag, for example, in the body here. And we could say Go to blog. And then for the Href of this anchor tag, this is where we're going to use the Jinja template to build out the href. So we're going to add the curly braces in and dynamically work out the href. And in every Jinja template, we have access to a method called url_for. So we can say url_for, and then because this is Python, we can add some parameters when we call this method. And what it's expecting is the name of a function in your Flask server. So you could, for example, hit up home or guess or blog. And in our case, this blog is what we want. So to make it right a little bit more clear because we've got the route which is called /blog, and we've got the function which is called blog. I'm going to change this to get_blog. So once you render this blog page, we can call this method get_blog by saying URL for, and then passing a string. So because we've got some quotation marks around the outside, we're going to use some single quotes on the inside. And in between a single quotes is the name of that method, get_blog, like this. Now, what it's going to do is it's going to generate a hyperlink that's going to be based on what it takes to get to this particular route and call this particular method. So now if I go ahead and update this and go to my homepage here, you'll see there's a new link that says go to blog. And when I click on it, it takes me to the blog page. Now, another thing that you might want to do is when you navigate to a URL inside your web app, you might want to add in some parameters. You can add parameters when you are using url_for in the same way that you did it when you did render_template. So that you can create the name of the parameter and the value and it is a keyword argument that comes after the first parameter. So here we could say, for example, url_for get_blog, and then we could just say a number equals three. So now when the user clicks on this anchor tag, it's going to look for a method called get_blog on our server.py which is right here, and then it's going to pass over any subsequent keyword arguments as parameters. So we can catch those parameters inside the app route. So we can say / and then we can use our angle brackets which we've always done to give parts of the URL a identifier, and we can call this num or number, whatever you like. And we'll also need to add that to the input to this method and just to prove that it works, I'm going to print it out. So now let's go ahead and rerun our code. And if we go back to our homepage and I click on go to blog and it goes to the blog website and it inserts that three into that part of the URL, and if I take a look in the console, you can see it printed out that number which got passed all the way from the index.html to the server. And finally, inside this method it was caught and it could be printed. And it could also be further propagated into another template if need be. ### What is Bootstrap?

Hey, guys. In this section, we're going to be learning about the Bootstrap Framework. And this is one of many external CSS layout systems, but this is probably one of the most popular and the one that you'll most likely to come across out in the wild. Bootstrap, as I said, is a CSS framework created in 2010 by two Twitter developers Mark Otto and Jacob Thornton. Now the power of Bootstrap and the reason why it became so popular is it contained pre-made CSS files, which you can simply include into your project in order to use their pre-built components and styling. For example, if you wanted to have some tags in your website, you could create a look like this by simply adding a few classes to your HTML. On top of that, one of the biggest reasons why Bootstrap took off is because of their 12-column layout system built on top of Flexbox that makes it really easy to create responsive websites and websites that simply just work and look great on mobile as well as desktop, the so-called, Mobile First approach. So how exactly does it work? Well, let's say you had a button which just said "Home", you can see that the standard button rendered from HTML doesn't look fantastic. But if we included just five classes which come from the Bootstrap CSS, so we include the pre-built CSS into our project and we add the styling and the components by adding these classes to our HTML, then all of a sudden what you'll end up with is something that looks beautiful and pre-styled like this. And because we don't have to worry about writing all of the CSS code, all we need to know is which classes we need to add to our HTML, then it makes everything so much easier and so much quicker when we want to build components into our website. Now, as I mentioned, bootstrap is a type of CSS Framework, what exactly are these? Well, they're pre-made CSS files which you can include into your projects. If we had a look at the Bootstrap GitHub and because Bootstrap is completely open-source, then all of the code is visible. And you can see it's got styling defined for all of the different components, for example, this is inside the Card Component and it's got classes that define what a card body should look like, what kind of layout it should have, what kind of color it should have, as well as what the card title should look like, subtitle, and it's got all of this predefined CSS, which we can simply insert straight into our HTML. Now, the two most popular external CSS frameworks are Bootstrap and Foundation, but there are lots more like MUI and Tailwind and a whole bunch more. And the reason why they're so great is because they allow us to add in pre-built components and develop websites quickly and efficiently. If we look at the usage percentages across the Internet, you can see that the biggest CSS external framework is still Bootstrap with close to 80% of the market share. But just because we learn about Bootstrap, it doesn't mean that everything we learned about CSS is null and void. In fact, if you look at the top here, when we look at the absolute usage percentages of all of the different frameworks across the Internet, you can see the largest percentage are still websites that don't use any external CSS frameworks. What does it mean when there are no CSS frameworks being used? Well, it means you're probably using native CSS like Flexbox and Grid and Float and all of the great things that we learnt before. So Bootstrap doesn't replace any of that knowledge and in fact, we should be in a situation where we don't actually need to depend on any sort of external framework. But, they are really useful when we want to develop websites quickly and easily and we don't want to spend a ton of time designing our websites, because it comes with all of the pre-made styling and all of the styling rules that we can easily conform to by using their components. So what are the pros of external CSS frameworks? Well, they're easy and they're fast to use and you get a ton of pre-built components like this Pricing Plan, which took us ages to build ourselves. And you also get really consistent styling across your website. It's almost like you hired a professional developer who kept everything looking on-brand. And finally you have really good browser compatibility because they've tested all of the different browsers Safari, Chrome, Brave and whichever browsers that your user might be using. So you don't actually have to do all of this complicated testing. You can just trust that it works out of the box. Now, what are some of the downsides of CSS frameworks? Well, one of the biggest downsides is something called, Class Bloat. Remember previously we mentioned that it's a really good idea to separate structure from style, where we said that HTML is for structure, so adding in elements that describe what the purpose is, and CSS is for style. Using external CSS frameworks, because we're adding everything into the classes, then very quickly you end up with what's called class bloat, where you have a lot of styling going into the actual HTML file and it looks a lot less clean than if we had just used something like Grid or Flexbox, where we have all of our predefined classes and we go easy on the classes that we add in to our HTML file. The other downside is customization. If you want to build a website where you want to have full control over every pixel and layout and everything to be exactly the way you designed it, then external CSS frameworks is probably not the way to go because in order to customize each and every component, it can be really time consuming. So when should you use the CSS frameworks like Bootstrap and when should you not? Well, when you are building a mobile-first responsive website that you want to put online very quickly and access beautiful components designed by professional designers, keeping everything on your website looking slick and uniform, then you probably want to consider using Bootstrap. But if you're building a very simple website, where you just need HTML and CSS and you can quickly throw it up, or if you're building a really complex custom design website and you want complete control over the design, then it's probably not a good idea to use an external CSS framework like Bootstrap. So we've spoken so much about the pros and cons, when to use, when not to use, but how do you actually use it? Well, one of the easiest ways is to include it via a CDN link. We've seen how we can use the link tag in order to add our stylesheets, and in a similar way, we can use these link tags that simply gets hold of the stylesheet from an external resource. So in this case it's through CDN, which stands for Content Delivery Network. And what these are is little hubs all across the entire world and it knows where your users are located. So when they load up your website and try to access this particular CSS file that contains all of the Bootstrap code, then it can find the closest location with the shortest distance to the server that has that content. And that just means that even though this has to be downloaded from somewhere, it can be delivered to your user and rendered very, very quickly. And from our point of view as developers, all we need to do is simply include this link into the head section of our HTML. And if we want any of the functionality like dropdown menus or clickable buttons, then we want to include the Bootstrap script just before the end of the body section. So somewhere right about here. Now let's go ahead and try an exercise and see if we can upgrade our website quickly by using Bootstrap. ### Bootstrap Layout

All right. So now that we've had a little bit of a taste of what Bootstrap can do, let's dive deep into one of the most powerful features of Bootstrap, which is the 12-column Layout System. The 12-column system is made of three components. Firstly, we need a div that has a class of "container" and this is going to be the starting point. Next inside that container, we need another div which is going to be of class "row" and inside the row is where we will have our items and they will be laid out using the column system. So what does this look like in code? Well, it's pretty simple. We have a container that contains a single row and then within the row we can have as many items as we like, and they're laid out using the column class (col). Pretty simple so far and you're probably thinking, well, there's nothing very groundbreaking here. Now, the interesting thing starts happening when you have multiple columns laid out inside these rows, because automatically Bootstrap will try to give every column inside the row equal spacing and space them across the entire width of the container. So if you had a container which included a row that had one, two, three, four, five, six divs in there, each with the class set as col short for column, then it will divide up the entire width by six. And if you had three of them then it would give each of them a third of the space. Now the bootstrap container is responsive. So by defining a div with the class of container, you're actually telling it to have a different size on different sized screens. If we had an XL or an XXL screen, so like a desktop or a TV or something, then that container is going to be this size and you can see that there's several breakpoints that are responsive to the different device screen sizes. On mobile, maybe the container would be 540px, on an iPad, maybe it would be 720 or 960px, and on desktop, maybe it would be about 1000px. You can use the dash (-) plus these different letters to specify at which point you want your container to be 100%. "Container-sm" is the same as the normal container, but "container-md" or medium means that on small screens the container would already reach 100% of the width of the screen. And again, remember, all of these sizes here are referring to the width of the viewport. So only this dimension. And then as we go down the line, we're starting to specify a 100% width on larger and larger screens until we reach this container fluid, which basically says that on all screen sizes, we want it to reach from edge to edge, which is 100% width. In most cases, you will see these two being used quite frequently because the container gives a nice sort of margin around the left and the right, and the container-fluid is when you want that edge-to-edge behavior. The layout system gets more interesting when we start using sized columns. Instead of just writing col as the class, we can actually set the class as for example, col-2 or col-4 and what this is saying is if we think of each of our rows as having 12 columns and we split them all up into the 12 equal size columns like this. So if you count this is actually a total of 12. Then when we create a div we can specify well how many of these columns do we want to occupy? In this case, this div wants two of those columns, and then this one wants four of them, and then the final one wants six. Based on the classes that you choose, Bootstrap will know how much space to allocate each div on a percentage basis. So you could view the col-6 as 50%, and the col-2 as one-sixth of the entire width and so on and so forth. So you can use all of the numbers col-1 all the way up to col-12 and you can split up the proportion of your screen and the content inside. So maybe you would have a navigation section on the left that you only want to take up 2 out of 12 width, and then the main content here maybe could take up 10 out of 12 of the width, and so on and so forth. And this is a really, really easy and intuitive way of sizing your content using Bootstrap. And this is what the code would look like, so we have three divs and we're giving this one 2 out of 12, 4 out of 12, 6 out of 12, and this is the layout that we end up with and we didn't have to write any CSS. All we had to do was add in the pre-built layout classes. Again, it's really important to know that Bootstrap has predefined breakpoints and these dimensions are defined based on common screen-sizes. And even though these numbers are constantly changing, generally I would say that small is for mobile devices, medium is for tablets and iPads. A large is for laptop, extra large is for desktop, and extra extra large is for anything crazy like maybe a TV or something. And extra small is for devices that are maybe longer than they are wide. So maybe foldable phones and even really narrow phone screens. Now, one thing I want to draw your attention to is the directionality of the signs here. All of these breakpoints, which will often use, for example, col-sm-2, this section refers to the screens which are greater than this dimension. So that means the small breakpoint is between here and here and covers the range between 576 and 768, and each of them always go up. So this is an important point to keep in mind when you're dealing with the Bootstrap breakpoints. Now, one of the great things about Bootstrap breakpoints is we don't really need the media queries as much because this covers pretty much a lot of the different device dimensions and we don't have to manually write all the pixel sizes, and add media queries into our CSS. We can target the different sizes and make our website responsive by using the pre-built breakpoints. Here's an example of the Bootstrap breakpoints. Here we're saying that on a small screen and above we want the dimension ratio to be two, four and six. So this means that on desktop, on laptop, on TV, it's all going to have this size. And even on mobile as well. But below the size of mobile, it is not defined as having these proportions. So it will default to giving each of these divs 100%. And similarly, if you don't add a number here. So we could for example, here it's 12 columns, 12/3, so these are actually col-sm-4's, but if we don't define a number, you remember that they will automatically distribute. But what would it look like if we reduce the screen size to less than a mobile size? Well, all of these divs will go to 100% width. When the overall width is less than 576, then all of these items default to as if they just had a column defined. So col as the class and the col class by default is going to take up 100% of the width in the small-sized screen. Now in a single div, you can actually also have multiple breakpoints. So in this case, what it's saying is on the large devices and above, then it should take up four out of 12 of the width. On medium sizes and above, well, because the above is already defined, so then this case is only on medium devices, then it should take 8 out of 12 of the width and on small devices it should take up 12 out of 12. So full width. Here we're simulating a large screen. So maybe on a laptop or a desktop, then it's taking up 4 out of 12. It's this kind of proportion. And then we go over to the next size down. So on an iPad, then it's going to take up 8 out of 12 of the screen. And just for example sakes', let's go down even further to a mobile size where we want it to take up 100% or full width of the screen. Because as you imagine, when we have more screen real estate, it's easier to see things, and when we're working on smaller screens, we want to make things generally a bit larger so that it's easier for users to see our content. In addition to having multiple breakpoints in each div, you can also mix and match the types of definitions. So for example, here we've got two-sized columns, col-2 and col-4. So it's always going to take up 2 out of 12, this section four out of 12 here, but this last one, notice how we've just left it as the column class. Now this means that it's going to automatically adjust in size in order to take up whatever proportion remains. Bootstrap layout is a little bit complicated when you're first working with it, and it's really important that you read the docs and also have plenty of practice before things start to make more sense. So in order for you to practice, I've created a website at appbrewery.github.io/bootstrap-layout, and if you go to this website you'll see that I've got three exercises in total for you. The idea of the exercises is that at the top there will be a demo area, which is the effect that you're trying to achieve. For example, in this case, we want these divs to be 50% on desktop and 100% on mobile. So as I reduce the width, you'll see that it gets to a point where we reach that sm breakpoint, where it goes into 100% width. As you scroll down, each of the different exercises will have different proportions, and what you want to do is to modify the HTML code inside here, which is responsible for the styling of the area that you control, which are the divs underneath the examples, and I want you to add the classes for using the 12-column layout system so that your area behaves exactly the same as the top-area when you reduce the size and hit the various different breakpoints. If you get stuck, be sure to check out the Layout Section of the Bootstrap Documentation and here you'll see the different Bootstrap breakpoints. Also, you can read up more on how the columns work, how the containers work, and how the grid system works. Pause the video now and give this challenge a go. Very often when we're designing websites, we will want to add margin, we will want to add padding, and this is all spacing, right? As you might remember from previous lessons, padding sets up the part between the item and the containing div. So this part and the margin sets up the spacing between the outline of your item and any other components. So you can set all of those values using very simple Bootstrap notation. So let's run through this quickly. It's a format where you have the property, which sides you want, a dash and then the size. And this is really easy to figure out. So for example, if I wanted to set margin only to the top of my element, then I can say "mt". So M for classes that set margin. T that sets margin-top or padding-top and then using a dash, I can say how much margin I want. So 0 is eliminating the margin and then we can add a little bit more, a little bit more, a little bit more. So if I had mt - 5, that's usually the maximum that you'll need. And then there's this concept of X and Y. So if you want to set the margin for both the top and the bottom, you'll use the x-axis. And if you want to set the margin or padding for the left and the right, then you can use that y-axis. So maybe you'll have my-3. It looks like my 3, but it actually says, "Set the margin for the y-axis to a size of 3." It's relatively easy once you understand it, but when you just see it in the code, it can be really, really confusing. But now you should be able to see that in our footer we've got mb-2 and that of course stands for adding margin to the bottom and it's a size of 2. That's how we can decode all this. Now, the only thing we need to add is just a little bit more margin. We should have a margin of 5 between these two sections and a margin of 2 between these two sections.
